name: David Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a builder that does house extensions and loft conversions in the suburbs. Right now it's a two-storey rear extension for a couple with twins, so I'm cutting the roof, fitting steel beams with the lads and planning the stairs into the loft. I start at seven, but I've usually done the day's cutting list at the kitchen table the night before with an AI app. I also do most of the client chats, because I can show them a 3D picture of their new kitchen on my tablet right there in their garden.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving the puzzle of an old house, where's the load going, how do we open this wall without the upstairs ending up in the lounge. What wears me out is planning permission and the waiting. On the side I own a mini-digger and a spare van that I hire out at weekends, which pays for the kids' extras. Sundays it's church with Hannah and the kids, then lunch at her mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's get going. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it's a handy tool and that's it. I'd keep showing clients their 3D kitchens, because they love it and it wins jobs. Online I don't say much, maybe a post on the builders' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, I was looking forward to what came next. But it'd be good for the family, steady work, steady money. Hannah does the books at the farm supply store, and that'd carry on too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep using the apps, keep the digger and van hired out, keep putting money away. Maybe I'd buy a second mini-digger, because the hire side is doing well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life, which isn't bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the 3D picture really help win jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loads. Last spring I won three extensions in a row against cheaper builders, because the clients could see it. One woman said she'd never understood a drawing in her life, but she understood my tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small, what would you still want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning office. Twelve weeks to approve a back extension is ridiculous. If AI could speed up the paperwork there, I'd be a happy man.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a handy tool and that's it, while continuing to win jobs with 3D kitchen pictures for clients. He might post on a builders' forum.
S0.think: Privately he'd be slightly disappointed, because he was looking forward to what came next. But steady work and money would be good for the family.
S0.do: Keeps using AI apps daily and keeps his digger and van hire going at weekends. Considers buying a second mini-digger because the hire side is doing well.
S0.feel: Calm, normal life, which he thinks isn't bad.
S0.quote: One woman said she'd never understood a drawing in her life, but she understood my tablet.
S0.fieldNote: David is an entrepreneurial tradesman who already uses AI to win business and runs a side hire business. He's a bit disappointed by the idea of a plateau. His frustrations are with regulation and planning delays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. On the forum I'd tell other builders to get ahead of it rather than complain. At church I'd say the same, in gentler words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do very well. Clients will still want a person they trust in their home, and if I can do the work faster with better tools, I can take on more. Whoever owns the machines wins, so I'll own some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd buy one of the robotic cutting machines that cuts roof timbers from a drawing, maybe twenty thousand, and hire it to other builders when I'm not using it. I'd ask my boss if I could run that side of the business for him, or else do it myself. I'd keep my savings, about a year's worth, untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really. It's like getting a new tool in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the lads on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train them up on the machine. Ollie's twenty-two and quick, he'd pick it up in a week. Old Pete wouldn't want to, and that's fine, he can keep doing the stairs by hand, there's still call for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government do anything in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly stay out of the way and keep apprenticeships funded. People who want to work will find work. I don't want the planning office regulating robots the way they regulate back extensions.

S1.say: He'd call it a chance for anyone willing to work and learn, urging other builders to get ahead rather than complain. At church he'd say the same more gently.
S1.think: Privately he expects to do very well, since clients still want a trusted person and better tools let him take on more. He believes whoever owns the machines wins, so he plans to own some.
S1.do: Buys a robotic timber-cutting machine for about twenty thousand in the first year and hires it out to other builders when not using it. Asks his boss to let him run that side, or does it himself, while keeping a year's savings untouched.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like getting a new tool in the van.
S1.quote: Whoever owns the machines wins, so I'll own some.
S1.fieldNote: His free-market outlook and adaptability combine into a clear strategy: own the machines. He would train younger crew and let older ones keep traditional work. He wants government mainly to fund apprenticeships and stay out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is big and fast, and families need to look after each other and get ready. I'd say the people who move first will be all right, and I'd try to help others move with me. I wouldn't be asking for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit unsettled. I can buy machines, but if AI can do almost anything, then the clients can buy them too, and why do they need me? My edge was being the guy who uses the tools, and in two years that edge is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go out on my own, with Hannah doing the books, and buy whatever robot framing kit I could get. I'd aim to be the local builder who runs the machines and talks to the clients, because people still want a face they trust. I'd sell the spare van to raise money and keep the savings as backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy, but with a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ben and Clara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben's twelve, he'd ask if I'd still be building houses. I'd say yes, with robots helping, and he'd think that's cool. I'd keep the worry for Hannah, at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. What about the people who can't move first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's where the church and the community come in. I'd give work where I could, and I'd hope others would too. If it got really bad, the government would have to help, I'm not stupid about that.

S2.say: He'd say families need to look after each other and get ready, and that those who move first will be all right. He'd try to help others move with him and wouldn't ask for handouts.
S2.think: Privately he's unsettled, since clients could buy the same machines and skip him. His edge as the tradesman who uses the tools would be gone in two years.
S2.do: Starts his own business in the first month with his wife on the books and buys whatever robot framing equipment he can. Sells the spare van to raise money and keeps savings as backup.
S2.feel: Uneasy, busy with a knot in his stomach.
S2.quote: My edge was being the guy who uses the tools, and in two years that edge is gone.
S2.fieldNote: Even this confident, adaptive man sees that if everyone can use the tools, his advantage disappears. His response is to go independent and own the machines. He prefers community help but is realistic that government might need to step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work. I'd push other builders on the forum to start learning now. I'd be upbeat in public, because that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build a proper business with machines and a name people trust. I'd be the one other builders hire when they need a robot crew for a week. I'm more excited than worried here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd buy the roof-cutting robot and start hiring it out. Year two, I'd go out on my own with Hannah, keeping my boss as a client if he wanted. I'd keep a year of savings and pay off the mortgage faster, because owing money when things change is a bad idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Focused, like at the start of a big job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be scrambling to buy kit before it's everywhere. With five I can build it properly, a business with a good name. Five years means I'm the one people come to, not the one chasing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Pete, and my brother-in-law, who drives a forklift. I'd offer Pete work as long as I had it. My brother-in-law I'd try to bring on as a robot minder, if he'd take it.

S3.say: He'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work and push other builders to start learning now. He'd stay upbeat in public.
S3.think: Privately he sees five years as enough to build a trusted business running machines. He'd be the builder others hire for a robot crew, and feels more excited than worried.
S3.do: Buys a roof-cutting robot in year one and hires it out, then goes independent with his wife in year two. Keeps a year of savings and pays the mortgage down faster.
S3.feel: Calm and focused, like at the start of a big job.
S3.quote: Five years means I'm the one people come to, not the one chasing.
S3.fieldNote: With five years his entrepreneurial plan comes together and his unease fades. He again plans to bring family and colleagues along through work, not handouts. He is careful about debt despite his appetite for risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and anyone who's not ready by then hasn't tried. I'd say it a bit softer at church. I'd push the local college to change apprenticeships now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is great for me. I'd be fifty-three, mortgage paid, a business of my own by then probably. I'd also have time to help Ben decide what to do, he'd be twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with my boss for a couple of years and keep the hire business growing. Around year three, I'd go out on my own with machines and a small crew. I'd put money into Ben and Clara's education funds, and maybe a bit into shares in the robot firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ready, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd go out on your own in the first month. Why wait now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years there's no rush. I'd rather learn on my boss's jobs for a bit, then go when the machines are cheaper. Smart timing, not fast timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Ben and Clara to learn by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to work hard and how to use whatever the machines are by then. And faith, and family, because that's what gets you through when work changes. Same things my dad taught me, plus the tablet.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is long enough that anyone not ready hasn't tried, though more softly at church. He'd push the local college to change apprenticeships now.
S4.think: Privately ten years looks great for him, reaching fifty-three with the mortgage paid and his own business. He'd also have time to help his son choose a path.
S4.do: Stays with his employer for a couple of years while growing the hire business, then goes independent around year three. Puts money into his children's education funds and some into robot company shares.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he slows his plans, preferring to time his move for cheaper machines. His values of hard work, faith and family stay central. He is the most comfortable of the AGI pictures here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my edge disappears before I can build anything. What would help is cheap loans for small builders to buy the machines, and apprenticeships that teach the new kit. Less red tape, honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about trust. People let me into their homes because they know me from church or the school gate. I don't think a robot gets invited for a cup of tea, not for a good while.

headlineQuote: I don't think a robot gets invited for a cup of tea, not for a good while.
portrait: David Ziegler is a 43-year-old lead carpenter on suburban extensions and loft conversions, married with a son of twelve and a daughter of nine, who also hires out his own mini-digger and van. He uses AI every day to plan cuts and show clients 3D designs, and believes whoever owns the machines wins. He's calm through the plateau and steady change, uneasy only under AGI in two years, when he sees his edge disappearing, and calm again with five or ten years to build his own machine-run business. He prefers community and work to handouts, but accepts government may need to help in a crisis.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his edge as the builder who uses the tools disappears before he can build a business.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small builders to buy machines, apprenticeships that teach new equipment, and less red tape.
